Can a jet break windows if it breaks the sound barrier far away from the building but then it flies by it? The short answer is: not likely, at least not in the straightforward way you might be envisioning. But then again, physics – much like our everyday understanding of the world – tends to be a little more subtle than our gut assumptions.  Imagine this: a jet breaking the sound barrier a good distance away from a building means that any shock wave or sonic boom it produces isn't concentrated right at the windows; it’s allowed to expand and dissipate over distance. That energy, once spread over a larger area, becomes considerably less potent. Windows, as sturdy as they are when manufactured for urban environments, have some capacity to absorb vibrations. They’d more likely rattle or vibrate than shatter from an acoustic disturbance that didn’t originate in close proximity.  Now, consider an alternative scenario: if the jet were breaking the sound barrier just over or right next to the building, then you’d have a much more concentrated force acting on a localized area, which could indeed be enough to stress fragile structures like windows. It’s the same principle as clapping your hands versus shouting across a room; proximity matters. Now, if one were to engineer a situation where the sonic boom path somehow focuses extra energy on a building’s façade—say, by reflecting off surfaces or by some peculiar atmospheric conditions—you'd be delving into territory more aligned with experimental physics than everyday engineering.   Honestly, it's one of those fun thought experiments where understanding boundary conditions and energy dissipation really shows off just how elegantly the fundamentals of physics explain phenomena that might otherwise be dismissed as urban myth. Ultimately, while it makes for a cool conversation starter and a neat illustration of shock wave behavior, a jet breaking the sound barrier far away from a building is unlikely to break its windows.

Having a new species require at least 2 mutated species (male and female) with same characteristics, and they need to be around the same area to have any chance of mating. If it is that difficult, how are there so many species on earth today? The idea might seem counterintuitive at first glance. I mean, on one hand you have this picture of evolution where a rare mutation in one individual—or a couple, if you will—must align perfectly with another mutation elsewhere, in the right place at the right time. Yet, when you look around, our planet teems with life. So how can this be? The answer lies in the mechanics of genetics, population dynamics, and plain old persistence over time.  Think of countless organisms living in wildly diverse ecosystems. In every niche, evolution is taking its slow yet relentless march. Mutations continuously arise—not in a grand single leap, but as tiny, incremental changes, many of which are neutral or only slightly detrimental or beneficial. Over generations, such subtle shifts can accumulate, sometimes leading to reproductive isolation. This process, known as allopatric speciation when populations become geographically separated, isn’t a sudden magic trick, but rather a protracted accumulation of changes that eventually lead to distinct, viable species.  Moreover, nature isn’t playing a zero-sum game here. There are millions of organisms interacting, mating, and adapting simultaneously. In such a bustling network, even rare events eventually have a significant cumulative effect. Adaptive radiation, for instance, demonstrates that once a lineage colonizes a new environment, natural selection can quickly diversify that group into multiple species, each exquisitely tuned to a particular ecological niche.  When you combine these factors—mutation, population size, genetic drift, selective pressures, and isolation—you begin to see how, even if the odds for a single mutation are astronomically low, the sheer number of individuals and the vast time scales allow evolution to work its creative magic. The diversity we see on Earth today is a testament to billions of years of dynamic, decentralized experimentation in the natural world.

So, while you may not see every “in-between” clearly marked on the timeline, the cumulative weight of evidence—from comparative anatomy to molecular biology—paints a robust picture of gradual transformation punctuated by branching divergences. Evolution isn’t missing intermediary forms; it’s just that nature’s record is far more subtle, fragmented, and, in many ways, far more beautiful than our simplified models can ever suggest.

What are the units of Einstein’s mass energy equivalence equation E=mc^2? If E were in Joules what would m be? If m were in ng what would E be? In SI, energy E is measured in Joules, which translates to kg·m²/s². That means the mass m must be in kilograms (kg), because c², with c being about 3×10⁸ m/s, automatically supplies the m²/s² part. No wizardry here, just unit juggling!  Now, if you’re wondering what happens when you swap mass into nanograms (ng), you first need to convert ng to kg. One nanogram is 1×10⁻¹² kg. Plug that into the equation, and suddenly your energy is E = (1×10⁻¹² kg) × (9×10¹⁶ m²/s²), which calculates to roughly 9×10⁴ Joules. That’s about 90,000 Joules of energy for the tiniest speck of mass—an exhilarating demonstration of how even minuscule amounts of mass pack an explosive punch.  So, no, there isn’t any weird mathematical black magic making the units unrelatable to normies. What might seem like sorcery is just the beauty of physics revealing itself through consistent, neatly defined units. At the end of the day, Einstein’s equation is less about magic and more about a fascinating translation between mass and energy—a language that’s universal and delightfully precise. At first glance, it seems like a contradiction, almost as if physics is playing a practical joke on us. Yet, the truth is beautifully simple when you consider the wall’s entire context. When you push on that seemingly stubborn barrier, you're not interacting with an isolated mass gliding freely through space. Instead, you’re confronting an engineered structure firmly anchored into the fabric of the building and, by extension, the Earth itself.    Newton’s 3rd law immediately steps into the scene: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. As you put your strength into that wall, it pushes back just as forcefully. But here's the twist: the wall is not free to respond by accelerating because its fixation to a far more massive system—be it the rest of a building, the ground, or even the intertwined lattice of construction materials—ensures that your applied force is countered at every point of contact. In effect, while your hands experience the impact, the net force acting on the wall is rendered nil, leaving its acceleration at zero.    It’s a bit like trying to push a mountain with a sledgehammer. No matter how fierce your effort, the mountain stands unmoved because its immense mass and the interlocking forces within its structure resist change. This everyday phenomenon isn’t a flaw in Newton’s law; it’s a vivid illustration of it. In our mundane interactions, from knocking on doors to battering down metaphorical walls in debate, physics is constantly at work in ways that both humble and enlighten, revealing the hidden order in the chaos of our daily lives.
